name: Muphry's Law
statement: Any criticism of someone's writing will itself contain an error.
meaning: If you publicly correct or criticise someone else's writing, spelling, grammar, or editing, you will almost inevitably commit an error of your own in the act of doing so. The critic gets caught out, and the deliberately misspelled name of the law, 'Muphry' for 'Murphy', demonstrates the point in its own title.
mechanism: Two forces converge. Heightened scrutiny: once you set yourself up as the corrector, readers examine your text far more closely, so any slip is both likelier to be spotted and more damaging. And irony: the correction is the very context in which an error is most conspicuous. A narrowing of attention onto someone else's mistake, at the expense of proofreading your own surrounding text, is a plausible but unproven additional cause.

examples.text: In 2008 the author Stephen Dubner suggested The Economist had printed a typo, 'pasties' for 'pastries', but 'pasties' was correct, readers invoked Muphry's law, and the magazine reportedly sent him a Cornish pasty.

In 2009 a newspaper attacked Prime Minister Gordon Brown for misspelling a soldier's surname in a handwritten condolence letter: then reproduced the same misspelling in its own coverage and had to apologise.
The everyday internet form: a post correcting someone's grammar that itself contains a typo. The archetype the law names, though any specific case is best left general to avoid misattribution.

variants.name: Skitt's law
variants.text: The internet-native twin: any post correcting an error in another post will itself contain at least one error, with the likelihood rising with the embarrassment it will cause.

variants.name: Hartman's law of prescriptivist retaliation
variants.text: A close relative: any statement about correct grammar, punctuation, or spelling is bound to contain at least one error (the same self-defeating trap, in the domain of language advice).

whyItMatters: It is the sharpest folk warning against the smugness of correction: a reminder that the moment you police someone else's writing, your own comes under a magnifying glass. Editors, pedants, and critics quote it against themselves as a hedge, and it is one of the most self-aware adages in the family, proving its own claim in its misspelled name.

working.text: since your critique will be scrutinised hardest, check it more carefully than the text you are criticising.
the law's real lesson is humility: public grammar-policing invites the exact humiliation it courts, so soften or sidestep it.

working.lead: Expect the trap in style guides too
working.text: per its corollaries, even books devoted to editing tend to be internally inconsistent; hold your own rules loosely.

limits: It is a humorous, self-referential folk adage, not a scientific law, and it is effectively unfalsifiable: memorable confirming cases get shared while the many error-free corrections go unremarked, the usual selection bias. It is not empirically measured; its persuasiveness rests on an intuitive attentional-and-embarrassment mechanism and vivid anecdotes rather than data. It is self-demonstrating by design — part of its charm, and a mark that it is a joke rather than a tested claim.
misreadings: It is not a measured tendency but a witty observation, and the attentional mechanism behind it is plausible reasoning, not an established finding. Its force is cautionary and comic, a hedge against the pride of correction, not a statistical law about error rates.
origin: Coined by John Bangsund of the Society of Editors (Victoria), Australia, in the March 1992 society newsletter, as 'the editorial application of the better-known Murphy's law'. His fuller statement adds corollaries: that a book thanking you for proofreading will contain mistakes, that the stronger the criticism the greater the fault, and that any book on editing will be internally inconsistent.

sources.text: Muphry's law, Wikipedia. — the statement, Bangsund's 1992 origin, the corollaries, and the Economist and Gordon Brown examples.
